title: Early Retirement Health Insurance: Options Before 65
metaDescription: Explore early retirement health insurance options before Medicare at 65. Compare COBRA rules, Marketplace plans, and income planning for subsidies.
h1: Early Retirement Health Insurance Options Before Medicare
cardBlurb: How to secure health coverage if you retire before age 65, including COBRA continuation rules, Marketplace plans, and subsidy planning.
introText:
To get early retirement health insurance before you qualify for Medicare at age 65, you can use COBRA continuation coverage, purchase an individual policy through the HealthCare.gov Marketplace, join a working spouse's employer group plan, or explore private coverage arrangements. At ModernWallet, we review early exit plans across hundreds of scenarios, and medical coverage is consistently the single largest cash-flow uncertainty between leaving work and turning 65. Navigating this bridge requires understanding how employment separation affects enrollment windows, how premiums change when an employer stops contributing, and how your taxable income influences potential financial assistance.

If you plan an early exit using our [early retirement calculator](/retirement/early-retirement-calculator/) or explore milestones through our [FIRE calculator](/retirement/fire-calculator/) (Financial Independence, Retire Early), your health policy decisions directly determine your required annual budget. Securing dependable coverage protects your accumulated wealth from unexpected medical events while keeping your withdrawal strategy intact.

sections.heading: The Coverage Gap Before Medicare
sections.body:
The coverage gap before Medicare occurs because standard eligibility for Medicare begins at age 65, leaving anyone who retires earlier responsible for finding independent health insurance. Under rules from [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/sign-up/when-does-medicare-coverage-start), your Initial Enrollment Period (IEP) begins three months before the month you turn 65.

Leaving work at age 50 or 60 means funding your own medical care for years. Going without coverage during this transition exposes your retirement assets to catastrophic medical bills.

To bridge this gap, early retirees generally select from four primary paths:

- **COBRA continuation coverage.** You maintain the exact group health plan you had while working for an employer with 20 or more workers, usually for up to 18 months.
- **Health Insurance Marketplace plans.** You purchase individual or family insurance through [HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/coverage-outside-open-enrollment/special-enrollment-period/) during an open or special enrollment window.
- **Spouse's employer plan.** You join a working spouse's existing employer-sponsored group policy during their open enrollment or after your qualifying loss of coverage.
- **Other private arrangements.** You purchase private off-exchange health policies, direct primary care memberships, or group association plans.

Each approach carries distinct rules regarding enrollment deadlines, network access, and out-of-pocket costs. Selecting the right fit depends on your target retirement age, whether you explore [how to retire at 40](/guides/how-to-retire-at-40/) or step back gradually through our [Coast FIRE guide](/guides/coast-fire-guide/).

sections.heading: COBRA Continuation Coverage Rules
sections.body:
The Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA) gives workers and their families the legal right to temporarily continue group health benefits after leaving employment. According to the [U.S. Department of Labor](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ebsa/laws-and-regulations/laws/cobra), COBRA continuation coverage is temporary health coverage for you and your eligible dependents that usually lasts up to 18 months.

The law applies to private-sector employers with 20 or more employees as well as state and local government plans. Enrolling in COBRA requires strict adherence to federal timelines. You have 60 days to enroll, starting on the date your job-based coverage ends or the date you receive your formal COBRA election notice, whichever date is later.

Cost is a major hurdle. Under the [U.S. Department of Labor COBRA rules](https://www.dol.gov/general/topic/health-plans/cobra), qualified individuals may be required to pay the entire premium up to 102% of the plan's cost. Because employers usually subsidize active employee health premiums, paying the entire cost out of pocket causes a sharp increase in your monthly cash outflow.

Your former employer may agree to cover some or all of this premium as part of a negotiated separation package. Absent such an agreement, you bear the entire financial burden yourself.

sections.heading: Marketplace Coverage and the Special Enrollment Period
sections.body:
Health Insurance Marketplace plans provide individual and family health coverage that you can purchase outside standard annual enrollment if you experience a qualifying life event. Under regulations outlined on [HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/coverage-outside-open-enrollment/special-enrollment-period/), you may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) if you lost qualifying health coverage in the past 60 days or expect to lose it in the next 60 days.

This 60-day window before and after coverage loss gives departing employees time to arrange seamless medical protection. Timing is critical when coordinating your departure. Retirement itself is not listed as a qualifying life event on HealthCare.gov.

The qualifying event is the loss of qualifying health coverage resulting from your departure from your job. Voluntarily dropping COBRA before it expires does not qualify you for a Special Enrollment Period. Similarly, choosing to stop paying your COBRA premiums does not grant you a new enrollment window.

When your COBRA coverage exhausts after reaching its full term, you gain a 60-day window to select a Marketplace plan. Marketplace rules also permit a Special Enrollment Period based on estimated household income. Premium tax credits depend on your estimated household income, reducing the net premium you pay each month.

In early retirement, your earned wages drop, which can create eligibility for these premium tax credits. Strategically managing taxable distributions, such as coordinating withdrawals with a [Roth conversion ladder](/guides/roth-conversion-ladder/), can influence your reported household income and your resulting subsidy eligibility. Specific income thresholds, eligibility rules, and available policies vary by location, so verify your details directly at [HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/coverage-outside-open-enrollment/special-enrollment-period/).

Because income definitions carry detailed tax consequences, consult a licensed Certified Public Accountant (CPA) or financial advisor to model your specific situation. This article describes general program guidelines and does not constitute individualized tax or financial advice.

sections.heading: Comparing Early Retirement Health Insurance Options
sections.body:
Choosing the best early retirement health insurance depends on balancing premium costs, provider network flexibility, coverage duration, and your projected household income. Each option addresses a distinct set of priorities during the gap years before 65.

COBRA provides unmatched continuity of medical care. You retain the exact provider network, prescription drug formularies, deductibles, and benefits you had while employed. This consistency is valuable if you are managing active medical treatments or have established doctors you cannot replace.

However, COBRA is limited to a maximum of 18 months in most situations. Paying up to 102% of the full premium makes it an expensive medium-term choice.

Marketplace coverage offers greater flexibility and long-term sustainability for multi-year retirements. Marketplace plans can remain in place year after year until you reach Medicare eligibility at age 65, provided you complete annual open enrollment renewal. Furthermore, Marketplace plans can qualify for premium tax credits if your estimated household income falls within qualifying ranges.

The tradeoff often involves provider networks. Marketplace options may use narrower regional networks, Health Maintenance Organizations (HMOs), or Preferred Provider Organizations (PPOs) that differ from your former employer's network. Joining a working spouse's plan represents an attractive middle ground that preserves employer group subsidies while avoiding the administrative limits of COBRA.

sections.heading: Transitioning Early Retirement Health Insurance to Medicare
sections.body:
Transitioning from early retirement health insurance to Medicare requires enrolling during specific federal enrollment windows to avoid lifelong late-enrollment penalties. Medicare does not activate automatically simply because your early retirement health insurance expires.

Under federal guidelines, your Initial Enrollment Period begins three months before the month you turn 65, includes your birth month, and concludes three months after your birth month. You can review the complete enrollment structure in our guide to [Medicare enrollment periods](/guides/medicare-enrollment-periods/). Deadlines are strict.

Understanding future Medicare expenses helps you establish accurate long-term retirement budgets. For context, the standard 2026 Medicare Part B premium is $202.90 per month, though high-income retirees pay more under federal surcharges. To explore how retirement income affects these calculations, read our guide to [Medicare Part B premiums and IRMAA brackets](/guides/medicare-costs-2026-part-b-premium-irmaa/) (Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount).

Failing to enroll in Medicare during your initial eligibility window while relying on COBRA can lead to expensive coverage gaps and permanent premium surcharges. COBRA does not count as creditable coverage for delaying Medicare Part B enrollment once you reach age 65. If you reach age 65 while on COBRA or an exchange plan, coordinate your Medicare start date carefully to maintain continuous care.

sections.heading: A Checklist Before Leaving Your Job
sections.body:
Completing a thorough health insurance review before leaving your employer ensures you avoid unplanned coverage lapses and unexpected medical bills. Preparing your transition well in advance allows you to coordinate termination dates with new coverage effective dates.

Before submitting your resignation, work through these essential discovery steps:

- **Consult your human resources department.** Ask about the exact date your active group health benefits terminate, whether that occurs on your final day of work or at the end of that calendar month.
- **Contact the COBRA plan administrator.** Request a formal estimate of your full monthly premium, including the 2% administrative fee, and verify how dependent coverage will be handled.
- **Review options on HealthCare.gov.** Compare available individual plans in your zip code, review local hospital and physician network participation, and assess potential premium tax credits based on estimated retirement income.
- **Speak with a licensed insurance agent or counselor.** Discuss local network quality and prescription drug formularies with an independent broker or a State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) counselor.

Taking these steps early gives you time to schedule necessary dental, vision, or medical appointments under your existing workplace benefits before your coverage changes. If you are assessing overall nest egg readiness, review our analysis on [whether $3 million is enough to retire at 40](/guides/is-3-million-enough-to-retire-at-40/) to see how annual medical expenses fit into long-range portfolio targets.

sections.heading: Coverage Tradeoffs and Plan Boundaries
sections.body:
Relying on self-funded bridge coverage is not suitable for individuals who have significant chronic health conditions requiring specialized academic medical networks that Marketplace plans in their area do not cover. Plan networks vary significantly by county.

If you require ongoing treatments at regional cancer institutes or academic research hospitals that refuse local individual Marketplace exchange networks, leaving a corporate group plan before age 65 can severely disrupt your care. In that situation, you should consider phased retirement, consulting arrangements that provide group benefits, or remaining employed until Medicare eligibility begins.

Our comparison between COBRA and Marketplace plans would change if federal legislation alters premium tax credit eligibility criteria, or if your former employer provides full retiree health benefits as part of your retirement package. If your former employer fully subsidizes your group health coverage during retirement, remaining on the employer-sponsored retiree plan almost always outperforms shopping for an individual exchange policy.

To protect your retirement timeline, review your local plan availability and confirm your estimated household budget before finalizing your retirement date. Establishing reliable early retirement health insurance keeps your wealth secure and guarantees continuous medical protection as you move toward age 65.

faqs.question: How long can you stay on COBRA after retiring?
faqs.answer: You can usually stay on COBRA continuation coverage for up to 18 months after leaving your job. The Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA) applies to private-sector employers with 20 or more employees. You have a 60-day election window to enroll, starting from the date you lose employer coverage or the date you receive your COBRA election notice, whichever is later. Because COBRA is temporary, retirees who leave work more than 18 months before turning 65 must transition to another coverage source, such as a HealthCare.gov Marketplace plan, once their COBRA period ends.

faqs.question: Can you get a Marketplace plan if you retire early?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can enroll in a HealthCare.gov Marketplace plan if you retire early, provided you enroll during the annual Open Enrollment Period or qualify for a Special Enrollment Period (SEP). Leaving your job and losing your employer-sponsored health coverage triggers a 60-day Special Enrollment Period before or after the date your workplace benefits end. Retirement itself is not listed as a qualifying life event on HealthCare.gov, so the qualifying event is the loss of your qualifying employer coverage. Furthermore, you may qualify for premium tax credits based on your estimated household income during retirement.

faqs.question: Is COBRA cheaper than a Marketplace plan?
faqs.answer: COBRA is rarely cheaper than a HealthCare.gov Marketplace plan because you typically pay the full premium amount plus an administrative fee. Under Department of Labor rules, qualified individuals may be charged up to 102% of the plan's total cost under COBRA. With a Marketplace plan, your net cost may be lower if your estimated household income qualifies you for premium tax credits. However, COBRA allows you to keep your exact workplace doctors, hospital networks, and benefit designs, whereas Marketplace plans may feature different provider networks.

faqs.question: What happens to health insurance at 65?
faqs.answer: At age 65, most Americans transition from private or employer health coverage to Medicare. Your Initial Enrollment Period (IEP) begins three months before the month you turn 65, includes your birth month, and lasts for three additional months. When Medicare begins, early retirement coverage such as COBRA or Marketplace plans ends or becomes secondary. You must actively enroll in Medicare Part A and Part B during this window to avoid lifelong late-enrollment penalties, as COBRA coverage does not count as creditable coverage for delaying Medicare past age 65.

faqs.question: Do you need health insurance if you retire early and are healthy?
faqs.answer: Yes, maintaining health insurance in early retirement is essential even if you are currently healthy. A sudden injury, unexpected illness, or emergency surgical procedure can generate tens of thousands of dollars in medical bills, which can severely deplete your retirement savings. In addition, going without qualifying health coverage leaves you without network discounts and subjects you to full hospital chargemaster billing rates. Securing continuous coverage ensures that unexpected healthcare events do not derail your long-term financial independence.
